description: Endpoints that attach a file to a user-controlled resource accept a user-supplied file id and attach it without verifying the caller owns or was granted that file; the attached file's content then becomes reachable by the caller.

A parsed-file delete operation is keyed by an integer file primary key with no user/workspace ownership scope; a manager/admin in multi-user mode can delete other users' parsed files in any workspace by enumerating the integer id.
Any authenticated user can delete another user's chat conversation by supplying its conversation id; the delete endpoint performs no ownership check.

A document retrieval endpoint checks that the caller is authenticated but not that they own the document or belong to its knowledge base; an authenticated low-privilege user reads other tenants' documents by id.
A key-management handler sets the authenticated user id and then spreads the request body over it; a body-supplied user id overrides the authenticated id and targets another user's stored keys.
Conversation select/delete/rename functions act on a user-supplied conversation id without verifying the requester owns it; an attacker can read, delete or rename others' conversations.
Due to an access-control gap, the first user created in the system can view, modify and delete chats created by an admin account.
An authorization check is incorrect, allowing an authenticated user to access resources beyond their intended scope.
An authorization flaw in the conversation-sharing path lets a user access another user's conversation.
Prompt endpoints fail to validate ownership; an authenticated (even read-only shared) user reads exposed prompt ids and overwrites prompts affecting all users of a shared brain.

In a multi-user RAG chat app, a regular user places another user's file id in the chat request's file-reference list; the retrieval path loads that file's content into the requester's own LLM prompt, even though the direct file-download API correctly denies the same id for that user.

After a user deletes a document, entries derived from it in the shared vector collection are not purged; a different user still retrieves the deleted document's content via semantic search over the derived store.

An id-manipulation flaw in a Notion OAuth integration causes another tenant's knowledge index to be populated with attacker-chosen content -- a write/poisoning effect that reaches the derived index layer.
